draft.title: Epidemiology
card: Epidemiology is the study of patterns of health and disease in populations. It looks at who becomes ill, where, and when, across groups of people rather than one patient.
Epidemiologists collect data from many people, such as how many in a region have a disease, and compare groups to find patterns.
Governments use these patterns to set health priorities. A condition that affects many people or is rising quickly may get more funding and attention.
The same data can judge whether a program works. If rates of a disease fall in the group a program targeted, that is evidence the program may be working.
draft.remember: Epidemiology studies health patterns in whole populations to set priorities and judge programs.

a.q: Which task is an example of epidemiology?
opts: Comparing rates of asthma between regions of a state
Treating a patient who has a broken wrist
Designing a training plan for a netball team
Advising one student on how to sleep better
a.why: Epidemiology looks at patterns of disease across populations, and comparing asthma rates between regions does this. Treating a broken wrist deals with one patient, so it is not epidemiology.
a.clue: Look for the option about a whole population, not one person.

b.q: Health officials in Tamworth run a program to cut smoking among teenagers. Two years later they compare teen smoking rates with rates before the program. What are they using epidemiology to do?
opts: Judge whether the program worked
Decide how much the program should cost
Treat teenagers who have lung disease
Explain why each teenager chose to smoke
b.why: Comparing rates in the target group before and after the program is using population data to judge whether it works. Explaining why each teenager smoked is a different question, because the rates show what changed, not each person's reasons.
b.clue: The officials are comparing rates in a group before and after.

a.best: Comparing rates of asthma between regions of a state

problems.detail: Why (b) explains that rates show what changed but not each person's reasons. That idea belongs to point 3 (Limits of epidemiology) and is taught here rather than only mentioned.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear correct answer that matches the card. The only issue is that the explanation for (b) teaches the 'what, not why' limit of epidemiology, which belongs to point 3.
